title: 486. Sets, Logic, Reasoning & Proof: Logical Statements and Truth Values
description: A comprehensive mathematics curriculum progressing from foundational numeracy and core mathematical concepts to algebra, geometry, calculus, linear algebra, probability, statistics, discrete mathematics, optimization, mathematical foundations of AI, advanced pure mathematics, and emerging research methods.

questions.learningObjective: Decide which sentence is a proposition.
questions.question: Which sentence is a proposition (a statement that is either true or false)?
questions.explanation: A proposition is a declarative sentence with a definite truth value. The sentence "\(7\) is a prime number" is true, so it is a proposition. The sentence "Close the door" is a command; it is neither true nor false.
questions.hint: Ask whether it makes sense to call the sentence true or false.

questions.concept: Truth value of an arithmetic statement
questions.learningObjective: Determine the truth value of a simple arithmetic statement.
questions.question: What is the truth value of the statement "\(2+3=6\)"?
questions.explanation: The sum \(2+3\) equals \(5\), not \(6\), so the statement is false. It is still a proposition, because it has a definite truth value.
questions.hint: Compute the left side and compare it with the right side.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why a sentence with a free variable is not a proposition.
questions.question: Why is the sentence "\(x+1=5\)" not a proposition when nothing is said about \(x\)?

options.label: A
options.text: It is false for most values of \(x\), and a false sentence is not a proposition.

options.label: B
options.text: Its truth value depends on the value of \(x\), which has not been specified.

questions.explanation: A proposition must be definitely true or definitely false. The sentence "\(x+1=5\)" is true when \(x=4\) and false otherwise, so without a value for \(x\) it has no truth value; it is an open sentence. Being false does not disqualify a sentence: false sentences such as "\(2+3=6\)" are propositions.
questions.hint: Try two different values of \(x\) and compare the results.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a declarative sentence from a question.
questions.question: Which sentence is a proposition?
questions.explanation: The sentence "\(5\) is an even number" makes a claim, and the claim is false; it is therefore a proposition with truth value false. A question does not assert anything and has no truth value, so it is not a proposition.
questions.hint: A proposition may be false, but it must assert something.

questions.learningObjective: Find the truth value of a general statement by looking for a counterexample.
questions.question: What is the truth value of the statement "Every prime number is odd"?

options.label: A
options.text: True, because \(3\), \(5\), \(7\), and \(11\) are all odd.

options.label: B
options.text: False, because \(2\) is a prime number that is even.

questions.explanation: A statement about every prime is false if even one prime fails the property. The number \(2\) is prime and even, so the statement is false. Listing several odd primes does not prove a claim about all primes.
questions.hint: Look for a single prime number that is not odd.

questions.concept: Truth value of a statement about irrationality
questions.learningObjective: State the truth value of a standard fact about a square root.
questions.question: What is the truth value of the statement "\(\sqrt{2}\) is an irrational number"?
questions.explanation: It is a proved theorem that \(\sqrt{2}\) cannot be written as a fraction of two integers: if \(\sqrt{2}=\frac{p}{q}\) in lowest terms, then \(p^2=2q^2\) forces both \(p\) and \(q\) to be even, a contradiction. So the statement is true.
questions.hint: Recall whether \(\sqrt{2}\) can be written as a ratio of two integers.

questions.learningObjective: Recognise that a false declarative sentence is a proposition.
questions.question: Which description of the sentence "\(10\) is a prime number" is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: It is not a proposition, because it is false.

options.label: B
options.text: It is a proposition, and its truth value is false.

questions.explanation: The sentence asserts something definite, and the assertion can be checked: \(10=2\cdot 5\), so \(10\) is not prime. The sentence is therefore a proposition whose truth value is false. Being a proposition requires having a truth value, not having the value true.
questions.hint: Separate two questions: does the sentence have a truth value, and what is it?

questions.learningObjective: Determine the truth value of a statement about the parity of zero.
questions.question: What is the truth value of the statement "\(0\) is an even integer"?
questions.explanation: An integer is even when it equals \(2k\) for some integer \(k\). Since \(0=2\cdot 0\), the number \(0\) is even, and the statement is true.
questions.hint: Apply the definition: an integer is even if it is twice an integer.

questions.learningObjective: Recognise a sentence that cannot be given a consistent truth value.
questions.question: Consider the sentence "This sentence is false." Which description is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: It is not a proposition, because neither truth value can be assigned consistently.

options.label: B
options.text: It is a proposition whose truth value is true.

questions.explanation: If the sentence were true, then what it says would hold, so it would be false. If it were false, then what it says would fail, so it would be true. Either assignment leads to a contradiction, so the sentence has no truth value and is not a proposition.
questions.hint: Assume the sentence is true and follow the consequences; then assume it is false.

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate an open sentence at a given value to obtain a proposition.
questions.question: For \(x=-2\), what is the truth value of the statement "\(x^2>3\)"?
questions.explanation: Substituting \(x=-2\) gives \((-2)^2=4\), and \(4>3\) is true. Once a value is substituted, the open sentence becomes a proposition. Using \(-4\) for the square, by forgetting that the square of a negative number is positive, would wrongly give false.
questions.hint: Square the negative number carefully before comparing.
